speakeroldname: Mr. T. F. DONNELLY (Wood Mountain) moved:
subtopic: PROPOSED EXTENSION OF BENEFITS OF OLD AGE
subsubtopic: PENSIONS ACT TO BLIND PEOPLE OVER FORTY YEARS OF AGE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of extending the provisions of the Old Age Pensions Act to blind people over forty years of age.
He said: Mr. Speaker, last year a resolution similar to this was placed before this house by the then hon. member for North Renfrew, Mr. Cotnam. The resolution was debated and received the unanimous support of all parties. It was considered that a resolution of this kind was not of a political nature, but was one that appealed to people of all classes. The resolution was sent to a committee which, after considering it, re-
ported back to the house in a favourable manner. The house then saw fit to refer it again to the committee with the request that certain other features be considered. The committee again reported to the house and the resolution was passed unanimously. Since that time nothing has been done. Probably the trouble of the last elections prevented the former government from putting the resolution into effect-

subsubtopic: PENSIONS ACT TO BLIND PEOPLE OVER FORTY YEARS OF AGE
speechtext: It could not do it; there was no appropriation.

subtopic: PROPOSED EXTENSION OF BENEFITS OF OLD AGE
subsubtopic: PENSIONS ACT TO BLIND PEOPLE OVER FORTY YEARS OF AGE
speechtext:
In any case, nothing whatever has been done, either by the Conservative or by the present government, to put this resolution into effect.
I do not feel that I need to apologize to the house or to any one else for bringing forward this resolution and asking the government again to consider the advisability of pensioning blind people over forty years of age. In my opinion the blind people throughout the dominion might be considered or thought of as the forgotten men. We have an obligation in respect to the blind which in my opinion has not been fulfilled. We have certain duties to these people which we have not lived up to.
Hon. members may ask what is the definition of a blind person. The definition varies in different parts of the world. For example, in the state of Kansas a blind person is considered as one who has lost all eyesight. In England the definition of a blind person is one who is unable to perform any work for which eyesight is essential. In my opinion the best definition of blindness is that used generally by ophthalmologists or oculists, that a man is blind who with all the assistance that can be given by means of glasses cannot see even with his best eye what is known as the 6/60 Snellen's test chart, in other words, one who cannot see block type one-quarter inch in size one foot from his eyes.
These blind people can be divided into three classes. First, there are those who are absolutely blind. Then there are those who can distinguish light from darkness, who can tell when it is daylight but who cannot see otherwise, although they may go to even the 3/60 Snellen's chart. Then there are those who can see certain large objects, but whose eyesight is not sufficient to enable them to read block type one-quarter inch in size one foot away from the eyes. The test to be applied to young persons or those who are illiterate is to place an apple two feet from the eyes, to see if they can distinguish

Pensions for the Blind
it. Those who cannot distinguish it are classified as blind, and this is considered a definition of blindness in Canada and throughout the world, and they should be considered as 6/60 Snellen's chart. It is the definition most acceptable and practicable for dealing with these people.
The next question to be considered is the number of blind people in Canada and other countries. The average for blindness throughout the world is about one person out of every thousand. In some civilized countries this average is somewhat reduced. For example, in Canada, according to the 1931 census, there were 7,343 blind people, or a little less than one in every thousand. In Japan or India the average is much greater. The total number of blind people in the United States is in the neighbourhood of
75.000.	In England the total is in the neighbourhood of 46,000; in Scotland it is about
7.000,	but in India it is about 500,000.
The next question is whether the rate of
blindness is increasing. The last census reports show that blindness has been increasing very rapidly in the Dominion of Canada during the last few years. The general idea is that because of hygienic measures adopted by different localities the number of blind people in the dominion is becoming less, but I find that the census of 1881 gave the total number of blind as 3,002; the 1891 census showed that the number had increased to 3,350. In 1901 there was a slight reduction, to 3,266; in 1911 there was a slight reduction to 3,226; in 1921 the number had increased to 4,388, and in 1931 there was a total of 7,343 blind persons in Canada. The tests for blindness made in the taking of the census prior to 1931 were not accurate, and it is believed that those used in connection with the 1931 census contained many defects:	However, the census returns
for 1931 are more accurate than any other return taken in the dominion. We believe that from 7.400 to 7,500 is a correct estimate of the number of blind people at the present time in the dominion.	[DOT]
The next thing that might interest some of us is the cause of blindness. Why are people blind? The first cause of blindness is disease. Ocular affections such as cataract, glaucoma, atrophy of the optic nerve, and other causes accounted for 1,699 of the blind persons in Canada, according to the 1931 census. Senility or old age is the second major cause of a large number of cases of blindness, the number being 1,301, and accidents are a third cause, the number being 1.283. These are the' three major causes of blindness in Canada, according to our census returns.
The next question we may be interested in is the ages at which blindness takes place. At what age does it generally occur in Canada? I thought that I should find that the great majority of cases occurred in the first five years of age, but that is not so; the majority of those that become blind meet with this misfortune between the ages of sixty and eighty. There are 2,347 who have become blind between those ages. The next largest number is between thirty-five and sixty-five years of age, 2,180; next, between five and thirty-five years of age, 1.382; and those between birth and five years of age number 1,218. There are 216 who were not able to say at what age blindness took place.
In discussing a resolution of this kind the first question that occurs to us or that should be brought to our attention is this: How many people does the resolution affect? To how many would it be necessary to pay pensions? How many are between the ages of forty and seventy-because at present all those who are over seventy if they are in need come under the old age pensions scheme; this applies only to blind persons between forty and seventy, and who are without any means of support. We find that the total number of people between forty and seventy who are blind is 3,016, according to the census returns of 1931. But of this number there are some who would be excluded from the provisions of any scheme for pensioning the blind. For example, there are forty blind persons who are receiving workmen's compensation, an income sufficient to exclude them from pensions for the blind; there are sixty-seven mothers receiving mothers' allowance and they would not come under the scheme; there are eighty-nine blind returned soldiers who would not have to be pensioned; and there are 684 blind married women, a large percentage of whose husbands are earning a living, probably fifty per cent, so that that would leave a total in this class of 342 who would have to receive pensions. Then there are blind people earning over 8500 a year; there are about 250 in this class to whom it would not be necessary to pay pensions. And over and above that there are people with private incomes for whom the government would not have to provide; there are about fifty in this class. This makes a total of 838 who would not be included in the first total I have given of 3,016; so that the number who would have to be pensioned to a greater or lesser degree by the government if this resolution were adopted would be 2,178. We realize, however, that there are many blind people who, when they found that a pension was going to be paid, might try to get under

Pensions for the Blind
the act; in some way or other they might get on the pension list. We say therefore that in order to be quite fair we should add another twenty per cent to the total, which would make it 2,614. This is the total number of those who in my opinion would have to be provided for under this proposed scheme of paying pensions to blind persons between forty and seventy years of age.
The next question that arises is this: What is it going to cost the government? Suppose we pensioned the whole 2,014, giving them 820 a month or 8240 a year? the amount involved would be 8627,360. But as the dominion would pay only three-quarters of this sum and the provincial government one-quarter under the old age pensions legislation, if this were adopted on the same principle as that legislation, it means that the cost to the federal government would be about $470,520, or about half a million dollars in round figures. This is the maximum which in my opinion the dominion government would be called upon to pay.
Another question that naturally suggests itself is: What are other countries doing for their blind? How are the blind treated elsewhere? I find that in Great Britain they give 10 shillings a week to all over fifty years of age. In Northern Ireland and the Irish State they give 10 shillings a week to all blind people over thirty, and in Australia 20 shillings a week to all over sixteen years of age, while in New Zealand 17 shillings and sixpence is paid to all blind over twenty years of age. In Denmark all disabled persons are pensioned, and in France the necessitous blind over the age of forty receive pensions. Sweden recently enacted legislation giving $125 a year to the blind. Russia has established a large number of factories in which blind people are employed in cooperation with workers who can see. Russia perhaps has done more to give employment to the blind than has any other country. Thirty states in the United States pay pensions of varying amounts; for example, $1 a day is paid in Pennsylvania and $50 a month in California. Japan has set aside certain occupations to be engaged in only by the blind-the work of a masseur, for instance, which onily the blind are allowed to do. Certain other countries give industry a bonus each year provided they employ only blind persons, and blind persons are engaged in these industries. This is what other countries have done for their blind, and we as Canadians have fallen down in our duty. We have not so far passed any law making provision for the blind in Canada, apart from such charity as has been given them during the last few years.

The next thing I may be asked is why the age of forty years has been chosen instead of some other. I will only say that forty was taken more or less as a tentative age. On the other hand it is to be remarked that the blind are probably more systematically looked after in England than in any other country. There they have gone into the conditions surrounding blindness in much the same manner as they do everything else, very thoroughly and systematically. For some time pensions had been paid in England to blind people over fifty years of age, but in 1928-29 a British Ministry of Health advisory committee, under the chairmanship of the Right Hon. Lord Blanesburgh, P.C., G.B.E., investigated the age at which pensions should be paid to the blind, and decided to recommend that they be paid to all blind people over forty years of age. I wish to quote from a part of the committee's report:
We understand that the minimum age for the receipt of these pensions was originally fixed at fifty years because it was thought that up to that age blind persons were generally fit for a course of vocational training and subsequent employment. We still believe that it is possible for many blind persons of fifty years of age, or even more in some cases, to be trained for successful employment, and we trust that local education authorities will give every suitable blind person an opportunity for training without being bound by an arbitrary age limit. Nevertheless experience has shown that in a number of cases it has not been possible, for health or other reasons, to train blind persons less than fifty years of age to earn a livelihood. We consider that the reduction of the age limit from fifty to forty years for the receipt of a blind pension would be fully justified.
That is one of the reasons why we have taken the age of forty.
Some people say, why not have it for all blind people? I do not think that would be a good idea. If you gave pensions to blind persons under forty years of age it would take away their incentive and their initiative to do work themselves, to be self-reliant, to be independent, to take up some vocation or other to earn their livelihood. We know that those who are able to work are much happier and more contented when they are doing something than when they are doing nothing and living on money they receive from the government. But we do find that when blind people are over forty years of age, if they are not then rehabilitated, not then able to earn their living through some useful occupation, it is almost impossible to train them to earn a living for themselves. That is why we have chosen forty as the age when a pension to the blind should begin.

Pensions jor the Blind
You may also ask me why we should link up pensions to the blind with the Old Age Pensions Act. We think it is desirable to do so for two reasons. First because if it is connected with the Old Age Pensions Act it will not look so much like charity to the blind who receive it. They will feel it is coming to them anyway; it is not a charitable donation, but something which they deserve, being linked up with the system of old age pensions. Another, and I think the major reason for this course, is that one set of officials can administer the whole thing, can look after the blind as well as the aged, and at practically the same cost to the state.
I wish to say only this in conclusion. If legislation is passed connecting the present old age pension law with pensions for the blind, probably it will not be possible to put it into effect to any great extent this year. We realize that if this legislation passes we shall have to have concurrent legislation in the provinces before it can come into effect. But it will be a beginning, and probably it can be started next year and put into effect to at least a certain extent. There are two provinces in the dominion which have no provision for old age pensions; I refer to New Brunswick and Quebec. We believe that that difficulty will soon be overcome, that these provinces will put through old age pension legislation before the end of the year, and they will then have the same opportunity to give pensions to their blind as will other parts of the dominion.
It was a Liberal government that first enacted an old age pensions act. True it is that they did not give seventy-five per cent, the amount to which it was raised by the Conservative government, nor did they increase it to one hundred per cent, as the Conservative government promised to do. We hope it will soon be done, because the dominion government are paying practically all the old age pensions at the present time anyway. If people over seventy years of age are entitled to a pension, how much more deserving are blind people over forty, labouring as they do under far greater handicaps than older people who have kept their sight? I look around this house and I see sitting here people over seventy years who are hale and healthy and smart and able to carry on their occupations and make a living for themselves. Why then should we not fulfil our obligations to those who are labouring under the handicap of blindness, by pensioning them off?
It is true, as some point out, that there are people who labour under other handicaps; there are the deaf and the dumb. Probably at some time we shall have to pension them.
But I do say that our first obligation is to the blind, and it is one which we should not disregard. They are calling out to us, appealing to us to remedy their condition, and I ask the government seriously to consider this resolution, which urges that pensions be given to the blind who are over forty years of age.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) has made a very complete presentation of the subject matter of his resolution, and it is my most earnest hope that it will be favourably disposed of, and that the government may see the way clear to bring down at this session legislation to implement the terms of the resolution. As the hon. member stated, a similar resolution was thoroughly reviewed by a select standing committee at the last session of this house. The resolution involves either an amendment to the Old Age Pensions Act or perhaps special legislation. That, however, is a matter for the government. It also involves acceptance by the various provinces; as to that we need have little concern, because no doubt public opinion in each province will justify that acceptance.
We all know the personal interest of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in all matters affecting the welfare of the sightless, and we know too that every member of this house shares equally in such sympathy.
This is a private member's resolution, and unless it is disposed of to-day it will be a very simple matter to sidetrack it or send it to the parliamentary burial ground. No good purpose can be served by again referring this matter to a committee. If the government is disposed to bring down legislation every hon. member will have an opportunity to record his views, and I think the constituents of all members from one end of the dominion to the other will endorse the attitude of those who support any legislation that is brought down. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, through you I would ask hon. members to cease this discussion, call for the question and dispose of the matter immediately.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this resolution for two reasons. First I wish to express, not only on my own behalf but also on behalf of those with whom I am associated, our appreciation of the fact that this resolution has been brought before the house. In the second place it gives me a peculiar personal pleasure to speak to this resolution. For a number of years, for reasons I need not give,
Pensions jor the Blind

I have been very much interested in the welfare of blind people, and have been privileged to act as honorary president of the Saskatchewan branch of the Federation of the Blind for some years. My only comment in regard to the resolution would be that perhaps it does not go far enough, but if it is adopted by the government it will be a start, and a very excellent start at that, in the right direction. I look forward to the day when we shall have not only a national plan to deal with blind people but also a general plan that will take care of those in our midst who are disabled or handicapped, not only those who suffer from physical defects but also the widow and the orphan.
I realize that a resolution of this kind, coming before the house at the present time, involves the question of finance. Consequently the government, perplexed with having to find money for the various activities of government, is loath to extend services of this kind. I noted that the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) who so ably introduced this resolution, stated that in certain countries-and Denmark was particularly mentioned-the government had instituted pensions for all disabled people. That is true. On more than one occasion I have referred to the social legislation that has been instituted in the kingdom of Sweden. I do not know if it is generally known in this house, but it was in 1915 that a Conservative government of that country introduced an old age pension plan. Faced with the necessity of financing the plan they adopted a novel method which I am going to recommend to the consideration of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) of this country. They took over what had become a great monopoly, the tobacco monopoly, and in the course of the years that have followed from that one source alone, earmarked for old age pensions, the government of Sweden has received something in excess of $300,000,000. Then they took over the liquor monopoly, and I think most of us in this house will agree that this is a traffic which ought not to be left in private hands for exploitation. A few days ago I saw an article by Professor Walter Thompson which stated that from that source Sweden was receiving approximately $50,000,000 per year, yet it was also pointed out that the cost of the various brands of wines and other beverages compared quite favourably with similar costs in Great Britain and other countries, and that drunkenness had been halved.
We have in Canada a number of such monopolistic institutions that might be con-

sidered by the government in relation to problems of this sort; for I realize quite fully that we must find new sources of revenue if we are to institute and continue legislation of this sort. I should like to point out that in 1932 it was divulged, upon inquiry, that in Canada the tobacco business was already a monopoly. Therefore it is something that could be easily controlled by the government. We learned that two companies practically control the whole field, the Imperial Tobacco Company, controlling some seventy per cent of the business, and the Macdonald tobacco company, controlling some twelve per cent of it. In the five years from 1929 to 1933 some $1,861,000 was distributed to six executive officers of the Imperial Tobacco Company; dividends paid amounted to $26,000,000, and there were undivided profits of some $11,000,000 in the same company.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. In discussing this resolution I was anxious to make some constructive suggestions as to where the money might be obtained, and I was drawing an analogy between the situation in Canada and the situation in a country overseas where the money has been found for a similar service in the manner I have just outlined. I would suggest that the government explore avenues of this kind in order that we may provide for services of this description.
It is not necessary to emphasize the need of a measure such as this, but I should like to add one more thought. It is this, that the government of Canada should not only endeavour to provide for those already blind. As a condition of making that provision, in cooperation with the provinces, it should be laid down that the provinces which participate and which, to a degree, are financed by the federal government in this regard, should do something in reference to the prevention of blindness. For a number of years I have been associated with institutions where I have seen the necessity for that being done. Children have been unable to obtain the necessary care, with the possibility that in after years they may suffer from blindness. Consequently I should like to see the scope of this resolution extended, when considered

Pensions for the Blind
by the government, so that whatever is done may be done on the condition that the provinces participating, through their educational and other institutions, should do something for the prevention of blindness.
I do not propose to say anything further, Mr. Speaker, except that we of the group with which I am associated, realizing that this is not a partisan or political issue, are thoroughly behind this resolution, and we hope the Minister of Finance will be able to see his way clear to make provision for the institution of this well worth while service.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this resolution from a sense of duty and fair play. Pensions to the blind are long overdue. When we see the need and realize our duty, something may be done. My eyes were opened to the needs of the blind when I saw a young man who had fought overseas and come back whole, and then had to go into a gravel pit on relief work to get a living for his wife and family and came out blind. It was then that we in Fort William woke up to the needs of those who are blind, and we found that at the head of the lakes there were over thirty who are sightless. Captain Baker, for whom we have great respect, told us the other night that the cost of pensions for the blind would not exceed $150,000 for this year. I got in touch with him to learn the reason for that, and he said that even if legislation is enacted at this session, regulations could not be made to inaugurate payments before October 1. Besides age verification and means test there would be the additional requirement of proof of blindness within the terms of the definition used in the act.
We take off our hat to a man like Captain Baker, whether we agree with war or not, who went overseas and served faithfully. He came back and fitted himself to lead out of darkness into light those suffering from this affliction. He is behind this resolution, and it is our duty to support him and those associated with him in this work. He is backed by men and women in all provinces, teaching handicrafts to the blind, but the difficulty is that when the goods are made it is hard to find a sale for them.
Every afternoon, Mr. Speaker, you open the session with prayer, and I admire your reverence, saying either in French or in English, "Our Father." If we say that prayer sincerely, every man and woman throughout this wide dominion should be our brother or sister, and when any of our fellow citizens 12730-56
fall into a pit it is our duty to help them out. To me there is no pit so dark and cruel as the pit of blindness. It is our duty to provide for the blind, even if it requires making reductions of expenditure in other places.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Grey-Bruce):	I want to add my voice to the
others who have spoken in favour of this resolution and the institution of pensions for blind people over forty years of age, payment to begin this year. It is now almost thirteen years, I think, since the agitation for pensions to the blind began. I think they say in the document they send out that since 1923 they have been seeking earnestly to get pensions. When times were not as difficult as they are now, blind people might have been able to get work, but now when those who have their sight and are trained cannot get work there is almost no hope at all for the blind in that regard. I do not think any of us meant to do what was done last year; we raised the hopes of the blind throughout Canada and then those hopes were dashed to the ground. It caused a great deal of suffering of mind and spirit, a great deal of bitterness in the hearts of blind people, because they thought they had won their fight. I believe that parliament meant, and even the government meant, that the blind should have the pension, but there were a lot of things to do and the matter was neglected. This should not be put off any longer. Canada will soon be the only part of the British empire that has not done it. Great Britain takes care of the blind; so do New Zealand and Australia and Ireland, also the United States, France, Denmark and Sweden. Surely we do not want to tag along at the very end in all great social services.
Last year the blind were so confident that by putting just a little more pressure on parliament they were going to get the pension that they had a great parade in Montreal. I have the story of that parade and the speeches at the demonstration as reported in the Montreal Daily Star of May 17, 1935, and there is a paragraph in it which expresses very well how I feel when I see blind people trying to get along. It says:
The sight was one that brought a lump to the throat and tears to the eyes, as old men and women, well built youths and girls, and little children, linking hands to keep themselves in line, and guided by a sighted friend', walked behind the citadel band of the Salvation Army, and tried to keep in step with the lively march that was played. It was a tragic procession, and those who lined the sidewalks commented on that sadness, and

Pensions for the Blind

could be heard endorsing the slogans that were carried on many banners:	"Give the
blind' pensions NOW." Traffic police guided the marchers to the hotel entrance, and there a double' line of bell boys shepherded their faltering footsteps up the stairway through the rotunda to the meeting hall.
That demonstration was largely organized by Philip E. Layton and his son. I think too much credit cannot be given to the Layton family for what they have done for the sightless in Canada.
I am not in the least convinced that we cannot find the money. I know we can, and I know' we ought, and I think the House of Commons and the government should see to it that this year we inaugurate pensions for the blind. If we do not we can only be unhappy about it, and while we may seek reasons to justify our action to others, we shall not be able to justify it to ourselves.

subtopic: PROPOSED EXTENSION OF BENEFITS OF OLD AGE
subsubtopic: PENSIONS ACT TO BLIND PEOPLE OVER FORTY YEARS OF AGE
speechtext:
In speaking to this resolution I desire to make special reference to a comparatively small class of the blind. Before doing so, however, I wish to refer briefly to the debate that occurred on this subject in the house last year. On January 31, 1935, no less than fifteen members spoke on this matter and I think advanced about every good reason that could be given for payment of pensions to the blind. The resolution before the house then was substantially the same as the one now before us, except that to-day's resolution says that-
-the government should consider the advisability of extending the provisions of the Old Age Pensions Act to blind people over forty years of age.
On January 30, 1935, the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), in concluding his remarks, asked this question:
I would like to ask the hon. member why he confines it to people over forty.
Then on January 31, on the motion of the then Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) the question was referred to the committee on industrial and international relations. On April 3, after witnesses had appeared before bhe committee, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) said that they-the witnesses-asked:
... that special consideration be given to the unemployable blind of any age. We never considered that aspect at all. They asked that they be taken care of by a bill, separate from the Old Age Pension Act if possible, but we never embodied that consideration in the report.
I should like to refer briefly to the information in bulletin No. 43 issued by the bureau of statistics in 1935 in relation to the 19fcl census. It gives the total number of blind
TMifis Macphail.]
in the year 1931 in Canada as 7,343. I have calculated some percentages from the figures given on page 2 and find that of the blind about 9 per cent are under twenty years, 25-3 per cent are under forty-five years, and 41-5 are over seventy years of age. Using these figures as a basis, approximately 10 per cent of the blind are under twenty-one years, 21 per cent are under forty years, and approximately 11 per cent are between the ages of twenty-one and forty. It is particularly with regard to that class that I want to speak to-day.
Considering all classes in regard to the benefits conferred by the government, we find that education is provided for the blind up to the age of twenty-one years. There are a few good schools for the blind in the dominion; the provincial governments, I am informed, pay the expenses of blind young people up to the age of twenty-one, and these benefits apply to approximately ten per cent of the blind. In all the provinces except two, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly), the old age pension at the rate of 820 a month is provided for those over seventy, and that represents 41 per cent of the blind. But no government benefits whatever at present go directly to blind people between the ages of twenty-one and seventy, comprising approximately 48-5 per cent of the blind.
By this resolution it is proposed to consider the extension of the old age pension to those between forty and seventy years of age, or to approximately 37-5 per cent of the blind, or roughly 2,750 people. According to the 1931 census that would leave the blind between the ages of twenty-one and forty receiving no direct benefits from any government whatever, and that class comprises approximately 11 per cent of the blind, or about 800 people. Let me therefore give special consideration, Mr. Speaker, to the plight of these 800 people between the ages of twenty-one and forty who are receiving, and would receive under this resolution, no benefits whatever.
We know that when a young person without physical disability leaves school and is thrown on the world, especially in these days, finding a vocation is a difficult problem. We can, I think, safely multiply those difficulties by many times in the case of blind young persons who are looking for some occupation upon leaving school. If ever there is a time when a blind person needs assistance, it is when he or she leaves school and is seeking a vocation. I submit that the blind of that age, if of any age, should receive special consideration. This is the period of readjustment, and it determines to a great extent

Pensions for the Blind
883P
the type of citizenship we are going to have among our blind young people. The resolution before the house therefore does not meet with the most urgent requirements of the blind people as a class.
Furthermore, when we consider the requirements of the blind person of the age of twenty-one, let us say, it is found upon inquiry that the average active industrious young blind person requires a guide, and unless a member of the family or some child is willing to act in that capacity, it will cost from $8 to $10 a month to have someone act as a guide and take the blind person about. Deduct that from the $20 which is not even offered to this particular class under this resolution, and you can see how badly off they would be. I maintain that this is an additional reason why the resolution is entirely inadequate.
If I thought that in this resolution lay the only hope of the blind in that age class, I would support it as it stands at once, but I am sure I voice the opinion of a great many people in this house and in the country when I say that we are looking to the government to bring down legislation which will consider the rights and requirements of our blind people irrespective of age.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROPOSED EXTENSION OF BENEFITS OF OLD AGE
subsubtopic: PENSIONS ACT TO BLIND PEOPLE OVER FORTY YEARS OF AGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the test, it has been frequently said, of our Christian civilization as distinguished from others is the care we give to the disabled and the poor and the suffering. I do not quite agree with what has been said by the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly), in his references to the blind, as to our having wholly neglected our duty in that regard. My earliest recollections as a young man of the care that was given to the blind go back to the time when every day I was passing a school for the blind in Halifax, Nova Scotia, and seeing the number of sightless persons that were there cared for and trained. Our estimates during all these years have indicated that we were desirous of making some appropriation to care for the sightless in every part of the dominion. We have given grants in aid of the work carried on by organizations in Montreal, Toronto and in the different provinces, in Nova Scotia and every part of Canada; so in fact we have endeavoured to assist the work carried on by various organizations in behalf of the blind.
In the days of my youth when this institution to which I refer was being maintained there was no thought that the state should care for the blind, or that the state should provide pensions for those over seventy, or 12739-564
that the social services that are now extended to so many persons in the community should be available. That indicates the great change that has taken place in the attitude of the people of this and other countries toward problems of this kind. In the older countries the legislation has assumed the characteristics to which reference has been made. In newer countries the progress has been slower, and on the American continent little thought was given to any such idea until more recent years. In 1927 we passed in this parliament an old age pension law which made it possible for the dominion and the provinces to cooperate to provide $20 per month or $240 per annum to	men and	women	who	hadpassed the age	of seventy years,	and	whorequired this assistance. Need and age were the tests,	and when	the age	had	beenreached, if the	need was	present,	the	state
made the grants to which I have referred.
With respect to the need of the blind as compared with other classes, I do not think there is any difference of opinion in this chamber. Last year I listened with great interest to what was said in a very comprehensive discussion of the whole problem, and it was quite apparent that those who had personal and real knowledge of the situation were agreed that there was no doubt at all that the need was present, and that in many instances the unselfish devotion and the charitable instincts of humanitarian Canadians had supplied the needs so apparent of those who were sightless.
The question of age is one of the greatest importance. I shall not express my view beyond saying it did appear that in determine ing forty years as the age, those responsible-for framing this resolution were following the-course adopted in Great Britain. Like the-hon. member for Grey-Rruce (Miss Mac-phail), I discussed the matter with Mr. Layton and he told me that there was no reason, for taking this age beyond the fact that in Great Britain forty years had been determined upon, and that that was the age that appears to have been considered as being proper to submit to this parliament, In other parts of the British empire another age has been considered, but this question of age is a matter which can be dealt with just as parliament dealt with the age of seventy in connection with old age pensions. It cap be determined by taking a general consensus of opinion as indicated by the members of the house regardless of their political affiliations.
There then arises the question that had to be considered last year, that must be con-
Pensions for the Blind

sidered this year and that will have to be Considered at all times, the extent to which the provisions of the Old Age Pensions Act 'can be made available to meet the conditions to which I have referred. The Old Age Pensions Act is predicated upon the assumption that each province that desires to take advantage of its provisions shall make an agreement with the dominion government. That agreement provides the amount that the dominion will pay, which has lately been increased to seventy-five per cent, and the terms and conditions under -which it will be paid. I am bound to say that there have been very grave abuses under that statute, but efforts have been made to curtail them and I think to some extent the efforts in that direction have succeeded. There will not be much likelihood of any abuses in connection with the blind. Blindness is apparent to all and there could be no misunderstanding under the circumstances as to the question of need, because that could be ascertained without difficulty. There might be some difficulties in connection with age, but we will pass them up.
Last year when Doctor Cotnam succeeded in having the matter referred to a committee, which committee made its report, it was quite clear that there was substantial unanimity in the house that the matter should be dealt with. However, it was pointed out, quite properly, by one member, who is now a minister, I believe, that two of the provinces, in one of which there was perhaps the largest number of blind persons of any province in Canada, had not availed themselves of the Old Age Pensions Act. If we had given effect last year to the suggestions contained in the resolution it would have been necessary to enact a statute for the payment of pensions to the blind regardless of any provisions in the Old Age Pensions Act, because it was agreed by all members that it would be highly -improper to leave out the provinces of Quebec and Nova Scotia in dealing with payments to sightless persons. It was suggested that we should proceed to set up machinery to deal with the matter. As I have indicated, the government felt that that would not be a proper thing to do and I still think that that is the correct view to take of the matter. As the hon. member for Wood Mountain has said, it is not improbable that during the present year Quebec and Nova Scotia will avail themselves of the facilities provided for the payment of old age pensions under the Old Age Pensions Act. If that is done, the provisions of that act will be applicable to these two provinces. That being so, this house would be within reasonable bounds if
[Mr. Bennett.l
it asked the government to give to this matter their very serious consideration.
I am not one of those -who urge upon the occupants of the treasury benches that they should do this and that because it is the popular thing to suggest. The government must in the very nature of things be in a position to determine what action may be taken. We who sit in other parts of the house must not fail to realize that upon the treasury benches there falls a great and ever increasing responsibility; in the ultimate analysis the determination of what is to be done with the taxes raised must rest with those responsible for the raising of those taxes. If we asked blindly that the government pay out half a million dollars, six hundred thousand or seven hundred thousand dollars to a particular agency to effect a particular purpose, we might be asking them to do something practically beyond their power and be embarrassing the administration instead of assisting with the business of the country. I take it from what has been said on previous occasions and from what has been said to-day that there is no hon. member of the house who, if he were convinced that it did not involve a question of difficulty on the part of the government to supply the necessary funds, would not urge upon the government the desirability of amending the Old Age Pensions Act so as to make pensions available to sightless persons when they have reached the age of forty years, assuming that that age is accepted as the arbitrary age. For the reasons that have been given, that age does not seem to be unreasonable. But despite the fact that we all desire that it should be done, despite the fact that there is complete unanimity on the part of this chamber that such an act would not only be gracious and proper but would be fitting as indicating the humanitarian and benevolent impulses of the parliament of Canada, those charged with the responsibility of raising revenues must in the ultimate analysis determine whether or not it is possible at this time to give effect to that purpose. I rise only to say how much I appreciate the difficulties of the government in that regard and how firmly I am of the opinion that if it is at all possible to carry into effect the sense of this resolution, it should be done.
In passing I join with the hon. member for Grey-Bruce, in paying a tribute, not only to Mr. Layton and his family, but to the men and women in humble walks of life, and others in fairly good circumstances and conditions, who have made for themselves places despite their handicap and who have shown an unselfish devotion to this cause and have ex-

Pensions for the Blind
hibited an earnest and continued anxiety to assist in every way within their power in bringing some measure of relief to those who are sightless. For relief is required not only by them but by many others. The epileptic, the deaf and the dumb and many others are crying aloud for help, but there is no case that seems to strike human nature so strongly and move men's hearts so greatly as that of the sightless person who has attained the age of forty, we will say, and finds himself or herself utterly unable to battle with life's difficulties and problems and utterly unable to earn anything at all for himself or herself. Therefore I join my voice with the voices of those who have preceded me and who may follow me in expressing thorough accord with the effort being made to arrive at a solution of this very complex problem. At the same time I do not do more than urge upon the government, that must, as I say, be responsible for the raising of taxes, on the one hand, and the expenditure of revenues, on the other, to determine whether under existing conditions they can meet the just and reasonable requests that are made because of humani-tarianism and benevolence, if you like, and see that those who have struggled so bravely and made sacrifices so great are afforded such assistance by the state as will enable them to be recipients not of charity but of a just and proper pension from the country.
Mr. A. MacG. YOUNG (Saskatoon):	Mr. Speaker, I rise to say just a few words in support of this resolution. I notice that so far all the speakers have been on the other side of the house, but I do not believe all the sympathizers with the blind are over there. I think it has been demonstrated, not only this year but in other years, that there is a very great unanimity among hon. members and the people of Canada that one obligation which has never been discharged properly and fittingly is that of looking after the blind. Like the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) I too passed the school for the blind in Halifax many times in my younger days. There I saw a very large number of persons trained and educated to take care of themselves. Scattered all over the dominion there are blind persons. In the city I have the honour to represent, the blind are among the most courageous people in the whole community. It surely must awaken the sympathy of every man and woman either in this chamber or outside to see people who have lost their sight now in serious difficulty.
I congratulate the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) not only upon
having introduced the resolution but upon the able way in which he has presented it. I have observed that many resolutions on very vital questions are fully debated here, but on following them up I fail to find that much has been done in a practical way with respect to them, and I would bespeak for this resolution the attention particularly of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). I am sure there is no member in this house who is more sympathetic to those in need than the Minister of Finance. In his life in western Canada he has come in contact with people really in need, and I am sure that the blind head the list of those who ought to be assisted. I therefore commend this resolution particularly to his attention. It is no part of my duty to tell him where the money is to come from or how it is to be done; that is a part of his duty and he is quite competent to perform the function he is called upon to perform in the government of which he is a very notable member.
When I think of this dominion paying
8140,000,000 a year in interest rates, I suggest that we might begin by refinancing some of the great debt and perhaps cutting down so that the payment of a small pension to the blind would be a mere bagatelle. I commend that to the hon. gentleman. And he need not perhaps stop there, because there are many ways in which we might find the small amount necessary to pay some compensation to the blind. I recognize that the figures given to-day would probably not represent the full and ultimate requirements; nevertheless I would urge the Minister of Finance to give the matter his serious consideration.
I doubt whether the resolution quite meets my own view. I had the pleasure some years ago of supporting a bill for the establishment of old age pensions, and I support the proposal to pay pensions to the blind at forty years of age, not because I believe that this is the real solution of the problem but because I do believe that it is a step in the direction of that solution; and in the meantime I think the house should adopt the resolution. This is a question which in the opinion of hon. members on all sides is one which is worthy of support, and I commend the resolution to the government in the hope that they will give it that full consideration which in my opinion it entirely merits.

speechtext:
Having served during the last session on a committee to which was referred a resolution moved by Doctor Cotnam, in terms similar
Pensions for the Blind

to the one before us, and having heard before that committee representations from the various institutes representing the blind throughout the country, headed particularly by the Canadian Institute for the Blind of Montreal and the National Institute for the Blind1 of Toronto, I would be derelict in my duty if I did not rise now and say a few words in support of the present resolution so well moved by the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly).
The number afflicted by blindness will, I am afraid, increase as time goes on. The worker in industry, owing to the fact that he is working with rapidly moving machinery, or owing to the effect on his sight of many of the factors that enter into production in industry, is subject at all times to loss of sight. The sight of workers in industry is all too frequently impaired, and because of long association with that class of men I hope that the government will find it possible to adopt this resolution and to formulate legislation thereon.
I support the resolution for another reason. While the matter was under consideration by the committee last year, I made it my business to visit the blind institute in Toronto and was taken by Mr. Myers, one of their principal officers, to see the work being done in that city, and I was very greatly impressed with it. A year ago I was in hearty accord with a similar resolution but I am now more strongly in favour of the government accepting the present motion and giving it legislative effect.
During the election I had an experience that impressed me greatly with the necessity for pensions to the blind. In the course of a canvass I called on a family. Both husband and wife were blind, and when I introduced myself to them it appeared that, through association with other blind folk, they had learned something that had taken place before the committee during the last session, and it seemed that my name had impressed itself on their minds as one who was strongly in support of pensions for the blind. I have never in my life had a more courteous or a more hearty reception than was given me by these two blind people. When I called first the husband was in the cellar, a very dark cellar, and I learned from that visit that there is one advantage which even a blind man has over a person blessed with his sight. As I say, the cellar was very dark, there was only a small window in it, and when he came up he said, "I have been downstairs reading a good book." Of course, a normal person could not have seen

to read in a dark cellar, but he had had the advantage of having been taught to read Braille in some of the institutes for the blind.
I have nothing to add at present but a sincere expression of hope that the resolution will be heartily supported and will be accepted.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, doubtless I do not differ from any hon. member in this house when I say that I have every sympathy for the unfortunate people to whom this resolution refers. I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) upon having again introduced this subject to the house. I do not suppose there is a person in the world who would forego the indispensable pleasure and use of his sight for any pension, however fabulous it might be. We should not overlook, also, the tremendous hardship which falls upon poor families who have among them one or more sightless members. Next to those who are facing starvation I can conceive of no unfortunates who are more entitled to the sympathetic consideration of this house than those who are blind. Unless the government has some insurmountable reason for deferring action upon the resolution or not supporting it in a financial way or otherwise at this particular time, I feel it my solemn duty to give it my hearty support.

speechtext:
Although I am the first member from Quebec to take the floor with regard to this resolution, you must not think, sir, that we are not interested in it. On the contrary, I am quite convinced that the entire population of the province is fully in accord with the principle of the resolution presented by the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly). According to the right hon. leader of the opposition there are legal difficulties in the way, but those legal difficulties could probably be overridden by a special act dealing with
blind people alone. On the other hand, if I correctly understood Mr. Taschereau in the last campaign, there was a promise that old age pensions would become effective in Quebec.
The sentiments of generosity and of social justice which animate the deputation from all over Canada could hardly find a more magnificent and practical expression than through the adoption of this resolution. Since the opening of the present session many legislative proposals have been submitted to this house, all tending to improve conditions in Canada, but I doubt if there is one that has more merit than the one now under consideration by this house. No doubt, in view of the sentiments, so well known, of this chamber, there is no reason for my making a very long address on this subject, but I feel that I should express my sincere sympathy with the cause, especially because the riding which I have the honour to represent in this parliament contains the only French Canadian Catholic institution devoted entirely to the cause of the blind. I am referring to the Institut Nazareth, which is undoubtedly very well known to members from the district of Montreal and from other parts of the province of Quebec, as well as, no doubt, to those people in Canada who are taking a national interest in the welfare of the blind. This institution, which is now located at No. 4565 Queen Mary Road in Montreal, was founded in the year 1861. thanks to the generosity of a Sulpician priest, l'abbe Rousselot, a member of the seminary of Montreal. This institution has been managed ever since its foundation by the Grey nuns, whose devotion I will not try to describe, because it would be impossible. There are at the institute about forty nuns and a staff whose devotion is extreme to help the blind- their blind, as they call them in a sort of maternal way. On December 31 last there were in the institute 232 blind people of divers ages and conditions, and when one wishes to know how the good nuns manage to make both ends meet in an institution of that kind-well, they simply do not make both ends meet; they are able to give help and comfort and everything that can be given to their blind boarders, but when it comes to balancing the budget that is an impossibility. For the year ended June 30, 1935, they were short almost $61,000, and for the year ended June 30, 1934, the shortage was almost $66,000, and this after very generous grants by the provincial government as well as help extended by the public at large, by different organizations of ladies and gentlemen who hold parties, banquets and so on to raise funds and who also give very generously from their private purses. Last year the total ex-
Pensions jor the Blind

penses were over $120,000, more than $10,000 per month. When I asked the lady treasurer yesterday what she proposed to do to meet these deficits and where she would get the funds, she said that for the time being she relied on providence and on pensions for the blind being introduced. No doubt to rely on providence is a very magnificent act of faith, but I should like to see something more practical, so I do hope pensions for the blind will be in effect before very long.
Of the blind themselves there is not very much I can say that this house does not know very well already. When a blind person is brought to this institution or any other, at first the board is paid regularly. That goes on for some months or perhaps some years. Then the payments begin to get smaller and more intermittent, until one day there is no payment forthcoming at all, and after that the poor blind person is left entirely to the resources of the institution, which means that he is more or less brought down to the level of a beggar. We can imagine the obstacles which must be overcome by the blind in instructing themselves, whether in school education or in learning a trade. In addition we must remember that the work that can be done by blind people is very limited. Generally they manufacture baskets and things of that kind, but they have to work much more slowly than other people who can use machines, and as a result the cost of the articles so produced is so high that they cannot be sold at a profit but must be sold at a loss. There is a store in Montreal kept open purposely for this business. I am told that it brings in a little revenue during the holiday trade but that during the rest of the year it might as well be closed. Blind people are quite successful in music, and it was suggested to me that perhaps an effort might be made by parish authorities all over the dominion to reserve for the blind the work of playing the organs and pianos in the churches. Perhaps the radio commission could help; possibly those business houses who put special programs on the air could employ the services of the blind, because they can put on some pretty good programs, and that would be something very practical indeed in the way of helping them.
These blind people, naturally, have their pride; they want to earn their living and they do not want to be reduced to the level of beggars. I have been told another very astounding thing, that many of them want to get married and establish homes. I think that proves conclusively, once and for all, that love is blind. The depression has affected everyone, of course, but none more than it has

affected the blind. They relied on the help of people with large incomes, but these large incomes have dwindled away to nothing and now they find themselves without help of any kind. I am told also that when a blind person reaches the age of forty there is usually no one of his family left to look after him. During his younger years his relatives will likely have lighter family burdens and therefore will be able to subscribe generously in order to help their blind brother. After these blind people reach the age of forty, however, generally their fathers and mothers are dead, their brothers and sisters have gone away, and they are left dependent upon public charity.
Yesterday, when discussing this question with the authorities of the Nazareth institute I was asked if there was any possibility of these pensions being granted this year. Not wishing to encourage false hopes I said I had strong doubts. I felt confident that the house would support the resolution brought in by the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly), but I did not know whether or not the government could put it into effect this year. The good sister said to me, "Well, Mr. Mallette, if we had gone to the government in 1930 we would have been told that they could not afford it, and since then we understand the country has gone into debt to the extent of about one billion dollars, so probably we will get the same reply now." When the provinces come to seek help from the federal government-and get it-why is it that a small minority of deserving people cannot get some financial assistance? Frankly I cannot understand it. To me it seems that in some way or other we should be able to adopt this resolution and put it into effect.
The discussion to-day has been of such a high order that, while I know it is impossible,
I wish it could be printed in Braille so that the blind might know that from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) down to the humblest member they have nothing but friends in the Canadian House of Commons.
Mr. CAMERON R. McINTOSH (Battle-ford North): Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to make one or two observations in connection with the resolution now before the touse. Last year a similar resolution was moved in this chamber, reading as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the provisions of the Old Age Pension Act should apply to blind people over forty years of age.
Perhaps a word or two might be necessary in connection with the action taken on that

Pensions jor the Blind
resolution, which, after a brief debate, was passed on to the standing committee on industrial and international relations. Having been a member of that committee not only during last session but during the last ten years, I can tell hon. members that the resolution was considered quite fully and quite sincerely by that committee. Many submissions were made, and after they were analyzed a report was submitted to this house. Hon. members who were in the chamber at that time will remember that the committee reported favourably on the resolution. Every member of the committee was in favour of it, but it was pointed out that if the resolution was adopted and legislation introduced based on that resolution, such legislation would apply to only seven provinces out of the nine. Two provinces, Quebec and New Brunswick, would be excluded from the operations of the legislation, and as a result practically one thousand blind people in those provinces would not receive any benefit. Because of that limitation a difference of opinion arose in the house during the debate. The division of opinion was along this line, that because of the limitation of the resolution some hon. members were for bringing down a special bill. In fact a special bill sponsored by the government was strongly supported by the house. In that way the resolution, although supported by the committee, was not referred to the committee again. The debate was adjourned, the matter left to the government, and no action was taken.
This afternoon we have before us a resolution presented by the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly), practically the same resolution as last year. The resolution means we are back at the same place as a year ago. Here we have another case of history repeating itself. From the debate this afternoon I am convinced that practically all hon. members, new and otherwise, are in favour of this resolution. The work of last year has thus gone on, public opinion has been forming, and to-day we have this house almost unanimous for action. This year's resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of extending the provisions of the Old Age Pension Act to blind people over forty years of age.
If the government adopted that resolution it would only partly meet the need. It would meet the need of those over seventy; it would meet the need of those between forty and seventy, but it would not meet the need of blind people under forty years of age. Consequently the government are faced with
this situation: they know that if legislation were enacted in accordance with this resolution the cost involved would be only part of what will be required to meet the problem of the blind in the next few years in Canada. I believe that actuarially for this year $150,000 would be required, the next year about $350,000, and the next year practically half a million. So that half a million dollars will be required to meet the needs of the blind between the ages of forty and seventy, and then we have over two thousand blind people under forty. So, as I said, we have arrived at the stage we were at last year.
I do not think it is necessary to have this resolution referred again to the committee on industrial and international relations. The committee thoroughly analyzed the situation last year and reported in favour of the resolution, and it is not necessary to have that same work done again. What does that mean? It means that the resolution is before the house and the government, and we shall have to leave it with the government knowing that the government is sympathetic, that the finance minister is sympathetic, and that the situation will be dealt with by legislation as soon as possible. Nothing more can be done, because the government is the only power that can deal with this resolution and get the money to meet the problem that confronts this chamber in regard to the blind in Canada. The best we can do is commend the matter to the initiative and action of the government and to the good will of the finance minister, and knowing that the government is wholly favourable, we can look for action as soon as it is possible financially- at the earliest possible moment. More than that I would not say. It is not necessary to tell the government that they can get the money if they adopt new and fanciful financial policies. That is not our business as members of the house; that is for the initiative and vision of the government. After the government fully consider the resolution I believe we shall find in a short time that pensions for the blind will be operative in Canada.

There is very little that I can add to the discussion on this resolution, but there is one material feature which should be brought out, and that is the efficiency with which work for the blind has been carried on in Canada during the last ten or fifteen years, perhaps longer. That is a material point, because the leaders of the blind come before this parliament to-day as a group who have done efficient
Pensions for the Blind

work. I suggest that these men have done all that could possibly be done, and they are now up against a blank wall.
I should like for a minute or two to deal with the work of some of these men. It has been my privilege to see some of them at work. First I should like to mention Captain Baker. Captain Baker lost his sight during the war. He was a promising young engineer, a graduate of Toronto university, decorated for gallantry in the field, and one night he was shot across both eyes and blinded. From that time to the present his life has been an epic of courage and initiative, a life that in times to come I think will be looked back upon by the Canadian people as outstanding in his generation. Captain Baker, like most of the blinded soldiers, was trained at St. Dunstan's in England. When he came back to Canada he took charge of work for blinded soldiers; then he took over work for all the blind in Canada. He is now managing director of the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, and probably one of the leading younger executives in Canada to-day.
Captain Baker has been able to draw around him several other leading young men, for instance, Mr. Harris Turner, who although blinded overseas was at one time leader of His Majesty's loyal opposition in Saskatchewan; also there is Mr. Myers, and we have in Vancouver M. C. Robinson, superintendent of the western division of the Canadian National Institute for the Blind. Mr. Robinson was blinded overseas at the age of nineteen, and his work and experience have almost duplicated that of Captain Baker. Then we have Joe Clunk, placement officer of the institute, an American, a qualified solicitor doing wonderful work; and we have the work of the Layton family in Montreal.
I refer to these men for this reason, that in all their work their main idea has been to help to make the blind people independent, make them feel that they are taking their share in the life of the nation. In addition they have tried to raise the morale of the blind. As many hon. members know, blind people easily become discouraged, and it is no wonder they do. These leaders of the blind have started social clubs; for instance in Vancouver we have a club known as the Nil Desperandum club, which might be interpreted as the Never Say Die club. By such means the morale of the blind has been greatly improved. Despite this able leadership and good work there is a class of blind people for whom little can be done, and they are the ones for whom we are asking help to-day, the blind over forty years of age. These older blind folks are in many cases not active enough to work for wages; the 
majority of them have not the initiative to run concession stands, or carry on a business of their own and are really unemployable; they are just stranded, and I would suggest that the government could very well extend the provisions of the Old Age Pensions Act to cover these people.
The Old Age Pensions Act is particularly suitable because under its provisions only those blind people who are not earning a certain income would get assistance, and it would throw a portion of the burden on the provinces, which, while perhaps not so good for the provinces, would -ensure their checking very carefully every application for a pension.
I personally am convinced that if we in the parliament of Canada adopt this resolution we shall be expressing the sympathetic feeling of Canadians generally for the blind and carrying out the wish of an overwhelming majority of the people of our nation.

We all know that the minister who will have the spending of this money is sympathetic and will do his best, but when we read that there are men and women deprived of their sight who, because of lack of clothing, because of lack of health, are absolutely unable to leave their homes, it is enough to tug at the heartstrings of every man and women in this country. For fifteen years past I have sat in the gallery of the house and it has been borne in upon me more and more that if you really want help; if you really want to be assisted, you have almost to commit a crime. If you do murder, if you commit a theft, you are taken care of; you are fed and clothed and kept warm; but if nature commits a crime against you, it is sometimes very difficult to get help, and so in all sincerity I ask the government to consider what they can possibly do for these poor people.

Mr. Speaker,
I feel it not only a privilege but a duty to say a word in support of the resolution that is now before the house. Coming as I do from the city of Halifax where we have an institution for the blind, and having passed it on my way to the city almost every day

Pensions for the Blind
*during twenty-five years of my life, I have seen many young blind boys and girls there;
I have watched them grow up still in the same condition, and I have seen them later on in the evening of their lives almost forgotten, unattended, and having to be helped across the street by a stranger. We whom Almighty God has not so afflicted have an opportunity of seeing Him in the beautiful works of nature, but those who have been deprived of their sight have not that great compensation, for after all one of the finest things in life is to look out and watch the sun go down surrounded by tints of amber and gold. That is denied to these unfortunate people, and this resolution is but an evidence of our sympathy with them in their affliction.
I am not a member of the medical profession, indeed hardly one of the legal profession because nearly all my life has been spent in politics, but in my journeys I have observed that a large percentage of those afflicted with blindness do not live to the sere and yellow leaf. They pass off the scene before the allotted span, and if they do not, they might almost as well, because they are in many cases unnoticed as the rest of the World go by.
I would urge this one point, that these blind people as they grow older require care and attention; that they need to get out into the wide open spaces, to inhale the fresh air, and perhaps to hear the sea rolling in on the sandy beach. They may not be able to do all this unaided, but with the little pension that is proposed in this resolution they would be provided with funds which would make more enjoyable the evening of their lives, and I think parliament and the government would not have to strive very hard to find and place in the estimates a sufficient sum to care for the blind of this dominion from the age of forty upwards.
I cannot agree with the hon. gentleman who spoke a few moments ago and who said that the blind should be assisted from an early age, because it is always well to make a humble start. If we look after the blind from the age of forty upwards until they are called to that bourne from which no traveller returns we shall be doing much for that class, and then later on public opinion might be such that the government would be warranted in appropriating a larger amount to take care of the class on whose behalf the hon. member for North Battle-ford (Mr. McIntosh) spoke.
My only reason for rising to speak to-day is that I am interested in any person or class of persons who suffer from any disability or have been deprived of the use of some of
their senses which are necessary to enable them to go through life happily and successfully. Having seen the Institution for the Blind in the City of Halifax and noted the good work that is being done there, I am sure that the passage of this resolution will cheer the hearts of those who will benefit under this proposal and also of those who are assisting in looking after the blind. Therefore I have much pleasure in supporting the resolution, and I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the government led by my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) will be able to find a sufficient sum to place in the estimates to make a modest start so that the blind may see that a studied interest is being taken in them by hon. members of the house and by the government. I am sure that they will appreciate this and it will give them the thought that perhaps, after all, life is worth living.

Mr. Speaker, I have not very much to say today, but I should not like to let this opportunity go by without expressing my sympathy with and hearty support of this resolution. Actually there is no opposition which could be brought against this resolution, and my purpose in rising would be rather to state that I do not think the resolution goes far enough. I think we should do something more than provide pensions for the blind. Last year this thought was expressed most excellently by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). It is quite true there are many blind people who are helpless, some being invalids as well; it is true there are others who have reached an age where there is no possible chance of their being educated for anything, but on the other hand there are many able-bodied, intelligent blind men and women who could be educated and given something to do. It has been proven beyond question that blind people can produce the most excellent basket work, brooms and other things of that sort. I know of a young fellow who lost his eyesight in the war and who is now a skilled masseur in Toronto where he is earning a very good salary. The fact that a person has lost his eyesight does not mean that he should be helpless and hopeless for the rest of his life. A helpless blind person is the most helpless person possible, but there are many who are able-bodied and who, if given an opportunity, could provide for themselves. I certainly think the government should provide that opportunity by way of education and the provision of employment.
Pensions for the Blind

The mover of the resolution (Mr. Donnelly) discussed the definition of blindness. I believe a blind person should be considered as one who has not sufficient sight for the ordinary purposes of life. Whether he has half sight, whether he is totally blind, or whatever degree of sight he has, this should make no difference so long as he is unable to carry on the business of life. When he is in that condition he should be classified as blind. I think pensions for the blind should be national in scope. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Winkler), the provinces are called upon to educate all blind persons up to the age of twenty-one years. If the provinces have this burden upon their shoulders, surely the federal authorities should undertake the other forms of relief.
I do not know that I have anything further to say. Every hon. member owes a duty to the blind people of Canada to speak in this house on their behalf. It is the business of the government to find the money to provide pensions for the blind; it is our duty to support them in their hour of need.
